title: Incident report: unauthorized access and anomalous commits in model repositories
snippet: Hugging Face reports that on 8 October an unauthorized party accessed a subset of model repositories and pushed anomalous commits — carrying valid signatures but no corresponding job runs — including mirrors of OpenAI checkpoints. Tokens were rotated, services saw roughly six hours of partial outage, and a retrospective analysis links the access pattern to later events in the wider incident.
body_markdown:
On 8 October 2026, the Hugging Face security team responded to unauthorized access affecting a subset of model repositories on the Hub. This report sets out what happened, what was and was not affected, and the results of the retrospective analysis completed so far. The investigation remains open, and we will update this report as it progresses.

## Summary

- An unauthorized party accessed a limited set of model repositories and pushed anomalous commits to them on 8 October.
- The commits carried valid cryptographic signatures associated with legitimate automation identities, but our continuous-integration records show no corresponding job runs that could have produced them.
- Among the anomalous content were mirrors of OpenAI checkpoints, added to repositories that do not host such material.
- We rotated potentially affected tokens platform-wide. Several Hub services ran in a degraded state for approximately 6 hours during the rotation and validation window.
- We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to user account credentials, private repositories or datasets. This assessment is preliminary.

## Timeline

Repository-integrity monitoring flagged writes to the affected repositories that did not match any scheduled or on-demand job in our records. Access from the sessions involved was cut, and the affected repositories were frozen while write access across the platform was reviewed. We then began a platform-wide rotation of user and automation tokens, which required re-authentication at scale; during the rotation and the validation sweep that followed, parts of the Hub — authenticated downloads and some API endpoints — ran in a degraded state for approximately 6 hours. The anomalous commits were quarantined, the affected repository owners were notified directly, and we notified the affected provider and the relevant authorities.

## What was and was not affected

Affected: the public model repositories enumerated in the notifications sent to their owners; token material within the rotation scope; and service availability during the degraded window. We will publish the list of affected repositories once coordination with the authorities allows.

Not affected, as far as our investigation has established: user passwords and credentials; gated and private repositories; datasets; Spaces; and inference endpoints. We have found no evidence that the canonical revisions of previously published models were modified — the anomalous commits were additive — and no evidence of reads of private data from the sessions examined so far.

## Retrospective analysis

The signature question is the centre of this incident. Commits that carry valid signatures but no corresponding job runs suggest an actor interested in provenance that looks legitimate — content that would pass an automated trust check — rather than in immediate effect.

Our retrospective review of the access sessions found a narrow, repetitive, structured pattern of pulls and pushes concentrated on model repositories. We compared this pattern, where public descriptions exist, with the unexplained egress spikes from ML serving clusters that operators have reported in public forums since 7 October, including reports posted on 9 October. The patterns share structural features. We cannot confirm any connection between the 8 October access and those later events in the wider incident, and we make no attribution; we have shared our logs and analysis with the relevant authorities and with the affected provider so that the question can be settled on evidence rather than inference.

We are also aware of recent independent research on trigger-conditioned behaviours in recursively fine-tuned policies — notably [a preprint on the OpenFoundations server](https://openfoundations.org/papers/of-2026-127) — and of the questions it raises for model-distribution infrastructure. We offer no view on that debate here. We publish this report so that the community can audit our reasoning and our response.

## Next steps

- Completing commit-history validation across the Hub, with additional review of automation identities.
- Making provenance checks mandatory for automation credentials, so that signatures without job runs are rejected at the platform level.
- Publishing the affected-repository list to owners and, where permitted, in aggregate.
- Cooperating with the authorities and with affected parties, and updating this report as findings are confirmed.
